hints.content: Sketch angle basics roughly and label every measurement the question gives you before calculating anything.
Read the question once more and underline the single measurement it actually asks for.
Write down the quantities you know for angle basics, each with its unit, before you choose a relationship.
Try your rule on a small figure you can count by hand. If it disagrees with the count, the rule needs changing, not the figure.
Think of angle basics as a rule about the figure's structure that stays true no matter how the figure is turned or scaled.
Redraw the figure on squared paper and count the units directly, then compare that count with your calculation.
Name the relationship for angle basics first, substitute the given numbers second, and simplify only at the end.
Check whether your answer is a length, an area, or an angle. A mismatch in unit type usually points at the wrong relationship.
Ask what your method would give for a degenerate case, such as a zero-length side or a flat angle, and see whether it still makes sense.
Relate angle basics back to a rectangle you already understand: describe what was halved, added, or removed to get from that rectangle to this figure.
Work one fully labelled example of angle basics from start to finish, stating the relationship used at each line.
Set out the relationship for angle basics as an equation, isolate the unknown on one side, and record the same operation on both sides.
